properties.snippet: This data set was created by Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) Contaminated Sites Program to provide the public easier access to contaminated groundwater plume information associated with contaminated sites.
properties.description:
This data set is composed of polygons encompassing the inferred lateral extents of validated contaminant detections in groundwater promulgated in regulations at 18 AAC 75 by the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (ADEC). Please note that there may be additional unidentified sources associated with groundwater plumes.

Defined Downgradient?

Uncertainty field which identifies if the plume has been delimited downgradient (defined in DQOs)

Defined Laterally?

Uncertainty field which addresses whether the lateral definition of the plume has been identified (defined in DQOs)

properties.licenseInfo:
The Groundwater Plumes Webmap depicts some, but not all, known areas of groundwater contamination in Alaska.  This webmap only displays select groundwater plumes that staff have entered.  The individual plume boundaries depicted are approximations based on groundwater data provided to the department and should not be considered definitive boundaries.  The actual extent of groundwater contamination may be larger or smaller and additional areas of contamination may exist that have not been identified. This map was developed using the best available information provided to the department and standard quality control criteria.

Additionally, the Plumes Webmap is only as accurate as the date it was created. ADEC receives additional groundwater data regularly. The plume data on the webmap will not be updated in realtime. Therefore, the webmap should be used in conjunction with the contaminated sites database, which is accessible on-line at the following URL: http://dec.alaska.gov/Applications/SPAR/PublicMVC/CSP/Search.  The contaminated sites database and the site files contain additional more detailed information, which may be more current.  ADEC recommends contacting the project manager assigned to an individual site if there are questions.

properties.snippet: Alaska is geothermally active with 97 known thermal springs. It is one of eight states generating electricity from geothermal energy. Alaska's first geothermal power plant at Chena Hot Springs has a generating capacity of 730 kilowatts and began operation in 2006.
properties.description:
Between 1979 and 1982, the Alaska Division of Geological & Geophysical Surveys (DGGS) and the Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska Fairbanks, undertook an assessment of the states geothermal resources under a program jointly sponsored by the U.S. Department of Energy and the State of Alaska. During this period, reconnaissance investigations of more than 100 thermal spring sites and fumarole fields located in Alaska were conducted by DGGS.

More recently, DGGS completed a cooperative project with the National Geothermal Data System on thermal springs and related geothermal data of Alaska. The Alaska geothermal database modules include comprehensive information on thermal springs, including temperature and flow rates, direct use, aqueous spring chemistry, physical samples, volcanic vents, geothermal wells, borehole temperature data and geothermal references.


DGGS developed and maintains an interactive geothermal web application that brings together various data services related to geothermal sites throughout Alaska.

  • Geothermal springs: Includes temperature and flow information. Spring location uncertainty and data sources are also included.
  • Geothermal wells: Location and name only
  • Volcanoes: Direct from the Historically Active Volcanoes of Alaska service

National Levee Database
 
This feature layer, utilizing National Geospatial Data Asset (NGDA) data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), displays levees within the United States. Per USACE, “The National Levee Database captures all known levees in the United States. It provides users with the ability to search for specific data about levees and serves as a national resource to support awareness and preparedness around flooding. The USACE is responsible for maintaining the National Levee Database and works in partnership with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and in close collaboration with other federal, state, and local governments and entities responsible for levees to obtain and share accurate and complete information.”

properties.description:
This layer is derived from the Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity in the Conterminous U.S. dataset hosted by Esri Federal Data and displays only Alaska features.

Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity in the Conterminous U.S.
 
This feature layer, utilizing National Geospatial Data Asset (NGDA) data from the U.S. Forest Service (USFS), displays severity as unburned to low, low, moderate, high, and increased greenness (increased post-fire vegetation response). Per the USFS, "The Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS) Program assesses the frequency, extent, and magnitude (size and severity) of all large wildland fires (including wildfires and prescribed fires) in the conterminous United States (CONUS), Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico for the period of 1984 and beyond. All fires reported as greater than 1,000 acres in the western U.S. and greater than 500 acres in the eastern U.S. are mapped across all ownerships."
 
Warren Grove Fire

candidates.title: Alaska DEC Drinking Water Protection Areas

properties.snippet: Drinking Water Protection Areas (DWPAs) are delineated areas around public water system sources created to meet the requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act. This map service is publicly available and is provided to promote the protection of public drinking water sources, with local governments and state agencies encouraged to use it when reviewing permits for activities that may affect a public drinking water source. DWPAs are divided into zones based on source type — groundwater, surface water, or groundwater under direct influence (GWUDI) of surface water — and can also be used to help determine sampling and monitoring requirements for public water systems.
properties.description:
Drinking Water Protection Areas (DWPAs) are delineated areas around public water system sources created to meet the requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act. This feature service is publicly available to promote the protection of public drinking water sources and also allows DEC staff to add the data to ArcGIS Pro for local desktop analysis and export. Local governments and state agencies are encouraged to use this data when reviewing permits for activities that may affect a public drinking water source. DWPAs can also be used to help determine sampling and monitoring requirements for public water systems.

The data is updated daily. Note that any data downloaded or exported locally is only current as of the date and time of download; regular exports are recommended to ensure you are working with the most current version.

Zone Definitions DWPAs are divided into Zones A, B, C, E, F, and G. Zone definitions vary depending on the source type: groundwater, surface water, or groundwater under the direct influence (GWUDI) of surface water. Note: Zone D (10-year Time of Travel) has been discontinued.

  • Zone A — Groundwater: equivalent to several months' Time of Travel. Surface water: 1,000-foot buffer.
  • Zone B — Groundwater: equivalent to 2-year Time of Travel. Surface water: 1-mile buffer.
  • Zone C — Surface water: equivalent to the immediate watershed.
  • Zone E — GWUDI: 1,000-foot buffer of the nearest surface water body.
  • Zone F — GWUDI: 1-mile buffer of the nearest surface water body.
  • Zone G — GWUDI: watershed contributing to the nearest surface water body.
  • Provisional Protection Areas — A 1,000-foot buffer around a regulated well or intake that is new or has not yet received a Source Water Assessment delineation.

For further information, visit the Source Water Assessment resource page. Users are also encouraged to use this service alongside the Alaska DEC Drinking Water Protection Areas Web Map.

Questions regarding this data can be directed to the DEC Drinking Water Protection Program at 907-269-7549 or via email at chris.miller@alaska.gov

Alaska DEC Drinking Water Protection Areas map service is a grouped layer that displays two data sources

This data should be used to promote protection efforts at the local level. There are currently  no regulatory restrictions associated with the Drinking Water Protection Areas. The data is being provided for informational purposes.

properties.description:
This layer is derived from the National Inventory of Dams dataset hosted by Esri Federal Data and displays only Alaska features.

National Inventory of Dams
 

This feature layer, utilizing National Geospatial Data Asset (NGDA) data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), displays dams within the United States, Puerto Rico and Guam. Per the USACE, "The National Inventory of Dams (NID) consists of dams meeting at least one of the following criteria:

  • Dams where downstream flooding would likely result in loss of human life (high hazard potential).
     
  • Dams where downstream flooding would likely result in disruption of access to critical facilities, damage to public and private facilities, and require difficult mitigation efforts (significant hazard potential).
     
  • Dams that meet minimum height and reservoir size requirements, even though they do not pose the same level of life or economic risk as those above – these dams are typically equal to or exceed 25 feet in height and exceed 15 acre-feet in storage, or equal to or exceeding 50 acre-feet storage and exceeding 6 feet in height.
     
The NID does not yet contain all dams in the U.S. that meet these criteria. Continued, routine updates to the NID and enhanced data collection efforts, focused on the most reliable data sources (primarily the many federal and state government dam regulatory programs), will help capture these dams and result in a more robust dataset over time."
 
Hoover, Davis & Glen Canyon Dams
